boxes.where: Cab side, close to the 61-pin, which now goes at the driver-side fuse-box hole. The exact spot waits on Dave.

why.text: Owner call: the ECU and PDMs go "somewhere awesome and safe". The 61-pin moves to the original fuse-box hole (driver side), so the ECU moves with it; the passenger-side spot below is superseded.
why.source: owner, 2026-09-29, in the pieces window (relayed by the pieces lane)

why.text: MoTeC's own limits make it a cab part. It is not a sealed engine-bay box ("protected location, occasional splash only"), it tops out at 85 °C, and it should not be bolted rigid to a vibrating panel.
Keep it close to the 61-pin so the 58 engine-wire tails stay short (HP Academy's tutors revisit wire sizes past about 300 mm from bulkhead to ECU).
why.source: K5_WIRING_STATE.md §1 rows 43 and 50; HP Academy forum (Zac Perston), via the pieces lane

why.text: The pedal's 6 wires and the dash switches never leave the cab. An engine-bay ECU would add 6 more firewall crossings.
Leave 60–80 mm clear below both plug faces for the Superseal plugs and their boots.

instead.why_not: The Four-Season duct and the radio fill that space, and every engine wire gets longer.
Header heat passes the 85 °C ceiling, it gets splashed, and the pedal adds 6 crossings.

open: What is behind the gold panel on the passenger firewall (asked 2026-09-29)? It decides whether the M130's plate can bolt there.
The bracket needs rubber isolators, not bare sheet metal.

boxes.what: Body power box (MoTeC PDM30), which feeds the lights, blower, wipers, windows and locks
boxes.where: Cab, in open air on its own plate near the M130, with an air gap between them. The spot follows the M130 (now open).

why.text: MoTeC says a PDM "may get very hot"; mount it where air moves and never against a hot surface.
It stays under 110 °C inside (100 °C recommended), which is about 85 °C around it at full load.
The PDM30 case is magnesium with only a coated circuit board, not a sealed lid. It belongs in the cab.
why.source: MoTeC PDM manual p.35 (Environmental protection); PDM30 datasheet

why.text: 29 of its 30 outputs feed cab and body loads, and its battery cable crosses the firewall in inches from the passenger corner.

instead.why_not: The Four-Season duct crowds it, and there's no airflow behind the kick-panel trim.
Longer runs to every load, and heat builds up under carpet.

open: Run it for 30 minutes and log its inside temperature over CAN before you call the spot final.

boxes.what: Engine power box (MoTeC PDM15), which feeds the fan, injector and coil rails, starter, fuel pump, A/C clutch and lambda box
boxes.where: The current design puts it in the engine bay. That breaks MoTeC's own spec (see why).

why.text: The PDM15 has the same unsealed case as the PDM30 (magnesium, coated board only). MoTeC's sealed PDMs are the PDM16 and PDM32, which have a rubber seal on the lid and the plugs.
why.source: MoTeC PDM manual p.35 (Case; Environmental protection)

why.text: A PDM16 would fit the engine job. It has 16 outputs (8 × 20 A + 8 × 8 A), 12 inputs and 100 A total, against the 9 outputs and 2 inputs in use today. It uses Autosport plugs.
why.source: MoTeC PDM manual pp.35–36; K5_WIRING_STATE.md row 0y (PDM15 outputs 9/15, inputs 2/16)

instead.why_not: Its engine feeds (fan, injector rail, coil rail, starter, A/C clutch, lambda box) would cross the firewall on the body pass-through plate. The fuel pump (rear) and the PCS trans computer (cab) get shorter.

instead.where: Engine bay, but as a sealed PDM16
instead.why_not: It costs more than a PDM15. Neither box is bought yet, so nothing is wasted either way.

open: Pick the PDM15 in the cab or a PDM16 in the bay. Nothing is bought yet (state row 0k); Dave's opinion counts here.
With Dave's one-connector rule (2026-09-29) the bay PDM would also carry the front-end loads, about 22–27 outputs, which points at a sealed PDM32. See the body pass-through entry.

boxes.what: Lambda box (MoTeC LTCD), which reads both O2 sensors and sends them to the M130 over CAN
boxes.where: Under the truck, on the inside of a frame rail near the two O2 bungs, a hand-width or more from the pipe

why.text: MoTeC says mount it "as far as possible from the exhaust"; it tops out at 100 °C around it.
The O2 sensors go at least 1 m downstream of the exhaust ports, tipped 10–90° from vertical with the tip down, never straight up and down. That puts the bungs under the cab near the transmission.
Never cut the sensor plug. Its calibration resistor is inside it, so the box has to sit within the sensor lead's reach.

open: The LTCD's lead length (the manual draws it in Appendix C) and where the bungs go (the exhaust isn't built yet).

boxes.what: Two batteries, the Odyssey for running and the Optima YellowTop for the stereo
boxes.where: Your working position is the passenger firewall corner

why.text: Owner's working position.
The factory Four-Season A/C box, which is locked to stay, mounts on the passenger firewall on the engine side. Both can't have that corner.

instead.where: Front passenger corner at the radiator support (the factory battery spot)
instead.why_not: The 2 AWG runs back to the PDM30 and starter get longer.

instead.where: YellowTop in the bed, next to the amp
instead.why_not: The amp's 18.4 ft cable loop goes away. The DC-DC charger then has to live back there too.

open: Which corner, now that the A/C box is going back in (asked 2026-09-29)?

boxes.what: Battery isolator (Blue Sea 7700), the switch that kills the truck, with its dash switch
boxes.where: Engine bay, on the Odyssey's positive cable as close to the battery as it fits. The dash switch goes in the cab.

why.text: Blue Sea says install it as close as possible to the battery, in a dry, protected spot.
It's sealed (IP66) and ignition-protected (ISO 8846 / SAE J1171), so the engine bay is allowed.
Owner told us to pick the isolator; the 7700 was picked.

boxes.what: Battery-to-battery charger (Victron Orion-Tr 12/12-30), which charges the YellowTop from the Odyssey
boxes.where: The current design has it by the batteries in the engine bay. Victron says it must stay dry (see why).

why.text: Victron says never run it in a wet place. Mount it standing up with the power terminals down, 10 cm clear above and below, near the battery but never directly above it.
why.source: Victron Orion-Tr Smart manual, safety precautions and §4.1 (Mounting)

instead.where: Cab, low on the passenger firewall face
instead.why_not: Its two cables cross the firewall, but it stays dry.

instead.where: The bed, if the YellowTop moves there
instead.why_not: None. It sits beside the battery it charges.

boxes.what: The 61-pin firewall connector (MIL D38999), the only thing through the firewall
boxes.where: Driver side, in the original fuse-box hole, on a CNC'd adapter plate

why.text: Owner call: "the 61 pin connector should be placed at the original fuse box hole with a cnc'd adapater plate".
why.source: owner, 2026-09-29, in the pieces window (relayed by the pieces lane; not yet repeated in this lead's chat)

why.text: Dave's rule: "the only reason to run a 61 pin is so you dont have any other wires going through the firewall. putting a bulkhead next to it is a problem."
why.source: Dave via the owner, 2026-09-29 (relayed by the pieces lane)

why.text: The factory fuse-block punch-out on the driver side is a 4 in hole, already in the firewall.

open: Plate drawing. The M130 moves with the connector, cab side, close to it (HP Academy's tutors revisit wire sizes past about 300 mm from bulkhead to ECU).
Questions for Dave (draft below, owner sends): the battery cables, sensor splices on the engine side, the isolator's switch wires, the rear connector.

boxes.what: Body pass-through (the book's "body bulkhead A, B, C and P") — DROPPED
boxes.where: Not used. Nothing but the 61-pin goes through the firewall (Dave's rule).

why.text: Dave, via the owner: "putting a bulkhead next to it is a problem." The four Deutsch plugs were an agent's placeholder (receipt 2026-09-27, decided for you, replaceable), picked because the kits were in stock, not on a builder's advice.
why.source: Dave via the owner, 2026-09-29 (relayed by the pieces lane); receipts/2026-09-27_whole-truck-body-circuits.md

why.text: Their 30 wires are mostly front-end loads (headlights, park/turn, markers, horn, wipers, washer, blower, underhood light, iBooster wake). A PDM in the engine bay can drive them from the cab switches over CAN, so none has to cross. MoTeC says a PDM input's state is sent over CAN and a PDM's outputs can be commanded by CAN messages.
why.source: MoTeC PDM manual p.19; k5_registry.json FIREWALL-BODY-A/B/C/P

instead.where: Front loads on a sealed bay PDM, switched over CAN (candidate)
instead.why_not: The bay PDM then needs about 22–27 outputs, which is a PDM32 (sealed, 32 outputs, 120 A). A PDM16 has only 16. It is not decided until Dave answers.

open: What still has to cross: the 2 AWG feed to the cab PDM and the ground returns (sealed cable clamps), and the isolator's 4 dash-switch wires. Questions for Dave.

boxes.what: Gauge box (Dakota Digital VHX control box)
boxes.where: Cab, driver side under the dash, within 3 ft of the cluster, both terminal rows reachable

why.text: It must be within its CAT5 cable's reach of the cluster, and Dakota warns against mounting it opposite ignition parts on the firewall. The coils are on the engine's centre mount, so driver under-dash is clean.
why.source: Dakota VHX manual MAN 650314:P p.4; COMPUTER_PLACEMENT_MEMO.md

boxes.what: Laptop ports (Ethernet for the M130, the MoTeC UTC plug for the PDMs)
boxes.where: Cab, under the dash or in the glovebox

why.text: The M130 tunes over Ethernet to a panel RJ45; the PDMs configure through a MoTeC UTC on a 5-pin XLR.
why.source: K5_WIRING_STATE.md row 0k (M1 Tune manual p.10; PDM manual p.48)
